summary: An April 1 joke RFC that defines a protocol for a Pi digit generation service between clients and servers. It is humorous and not a real standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke proposes asking network servers for digits of pi. It describes several ways to request or receive the digits.

subtitle: An April 1st joke protocol for requesting digits of pi over a network.

tldr.problem: This April 1st RFC jokes that computers without local pi calculation could ask servers for the digits instead.
tldr.mechanism: It describes TCP streams, UDP requests for particular digits, and a multicast stream of digits, plus an approximate service for 22/7.
tldr.outcome: PIgen is an April 1st joke protocol description, not a recommended service for real systems.

today: RFC 3091 is an Informational April 1st joke about serving digits of pi over a network.

sections.title: The PIgen Service
sections.content:
The RFC describes PIgen, a service for clients to receive decimal digits of pi from servers. It says the trade-off is using network resources and time instead of local computing cycles.

It is an April 1st joke presented as a technical protocol. The memo includes TCP, UDP, multicast, service discovery, and security sections.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to obtain pi digits over a network instead of calculating them locally. The straight-faced technical detail is the joke.

sections.title: TCP and UDP Services
sections.content:
The required TCP service listens on port 314159 and sends a stream of digits after the decimal point until the client closes the connection. An optional TCP service on port 220007 sends digits of 22/7 instead.

With the optional UDP service on port 314159, a request names the digit position and the reply contains that position and its digit. The RFC also describes an optional UDP service for requesting digits of 22/7 on port 220007.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP streams digits until the client disconnects. UDP lets a client request a particular digit and receive a short reply.

sections.title: Multicast and Service Discovery
sections.content:
The optional multicast service sends a random distribution of pi digits to the group address 314.159.265.359. A client builds a coherent value by listening over time; a server may begin providing digits if it detects no provider within 30 seconds.

Clients should discover servers through DNS SRV records using service names “pigen” or “pigem”. The security section jokes that clients must use a trusted server to prevent the imminent collapse of the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The multicast option broadcasts digits for listeners to collect over time. The memo also gives DNS service names for finding a provider.
